paras: The William Strickland peonage case was a federal prosecution in August 1905 of William Strickland, a Black farmer at Baconton, Georgia, accused of holding a Black boy, Henry Sterling, in involuntary servitude. Strickland was arrested by a deputy U.S. marshal, held on bond, and reportedly bound over to the federal grand jury. Papers treated the case as notable because the peonage law was being used against a Black employer, which a Macon dispatch called a first for the federal courts there.
According to the Associated Press report from Valdosta, Strickland had obtained the boy in South Carolina and kept him at work.

The same report claimed that Strickland whipped the boy, that the boy ran away, and that Strickland then had him arrested under the labor contract law. Strickland was said to have had the boy released on his promise to work out the matter and to have kept him in his service afterward. An earlier Macon dispatch told it differently, saying Strickland beat the boy when he ran away from his employer "with a small amount of money."

The boy complained to other Black residents, who "took the matter up" against Strickland. Deputy U.S. Marshal Godwin, spelled Goodwin in some copies, arrested Strickland at Baconton, and by August 17 he was being held in Macon on the peonage charge.

Strickland's bond was set at $300, and Sterling was held in jail as a witness at $1 a day to await the hearing before U.S. Commissioner Martin. In early September the Baltimore Afro-American reported that the court had bound Strickland over to the next term of the federal grand jury, in a sum that its partly legible text gives as "four hundred." No report of an indictment or trial was found.

The first report, a Macon dispatch of August 17, ran in Florida papers under the headline "Negro Charged With Peonage" and described the case as "novel" because a law "instituted for the benefit of the blacks" was being turned on a Black man. The fuller Valdosta Associated Press story, which named the boy, ran from August 23 in the Birmingham Age-Herald, the Montgomery Advertiser, the Richmond Times-Dispatch, the Raleigh News & Observer and smaller papers. Its headlines stressed race, as in "Negro In Georgia Holds Boy In Involuntary Servitude" and "The Charge is Brought Against a Negro for Holding a Black Boy," while the text hedged the charges with "It is claimed" and "according to the report."

The only Black-press notice found was a short editorial paragraph in the Baltimore Afro-American. Rather than treat the case as news, the paper offered it with irony as evidence that "the Negro is a close imitator of the white man, good, bab [bad] or indifferent," calling the boy's condition "involitary slavery."

The Macon dispatch placed the arrest "near Valdosta," while the more detailed Valdosta report named Baconton. The bond also differs, $300 in the Associated Press report and "four hundred" in the Afro-American, though the latter accompanies a later binding over and may refer to a different stage.

reader.title: William Strickland peonage case
bases: Strickland was arrested by federal officers on a charge of violating the peonage law for holding a boy in 'involuntary servitude' (A2, A7, A11).

An Aug 17 Macon dispatch (A2), a separate Aug 22 Valdosta AP report (A4, A7), and the Baltimore Afro-American (A11) agree that Strickland was held on a peonage charge for keeping a Black boy in servitude.

accounts.label: Macon dispatch
accounts.gist: A Black farmer arrested near Valdosta was held in Macon for holding a Black boy in servitude and beating him when he ran away with a small amount of money; a hearing before Commissioner Martin was to follow.

accounts.label: Valdosta AP report
accounts.gist: Deputy Marshal Godwin arrested Strickland at Baconton; Strickland had brought Henry Sterling from South Carolina, whipped him, had him arrested under the labor contract law when he ran away, and held him in service; other Black residents took up the boy's complaint.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: The Afro-American reported the court bound Strickland over to the federal grand jury for holding a 16-year-old in 'involitary slavery'.

framing.detail: The Macon dispatch, headlined 'Negro Charged With Peonage', stressed that a law 'instituted for the benefit of the blacks' was being used against a Black man for the first time in the federal courts there.

The Valdosta AP story ran from Alabama to Virginia and North Carolina under headlines such as 'Negro In Georgia Holds Boy In Involuntary Servitude' and 'Accused of Peonage', attributing the charges with 'It is claimed' and 'according to the report'.
The Afro-American treated the case ironically, as proof that 'the Negro is a close imitator of the white man, good, bab or indifferent'.

conflicts.note: The later, more detailed Valdosta AP report names Baconton as the place of arrest; the Macon dispatch gives only 'near Valdosta'.

versions.value: beaten when he ran away from his employer with a small amount of money
whipped, after which he ran away and was arrested under the labor contract law

conflicts.note: The two dispatches differ on the order of beating and flight; only the Macon dispatch mentions money.
The AP bond was set before the hearing; the Afro-American figure accompanies its report of a binding over, so the two may refer to different stages.

info: Arrest date not stated; Strickland was already held in Macon by Aug 17, and an Aug 22 Valdosta report said the deputy marshal had returned from making the arrest.
Baconton (also 'Bacontown'), per the Valdosta AP report; the Macon dispatch says 'near Valdosta'.
Henry Sterling, a Black boy brought from South Carolina; 16 years old per the Afro-American.
Charged with violating the federal peonage law by holding the boy in 'involuntary servitude'.
William Strickland, described as a 'negro farmer' (white press) and a 'colored man' (Afro-American).
